reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
clinicalPearls: Results from sustained venous hypertension due to valvular incompetence (reflux), venous obstruction, or calf-muscle pump failure, or a combination of these
The clinical spectrum runs from telangiectasia and varicose veins to oedema, skin changes (haemosiderin pigmentation, venous eczema, lipodermatosclerosis, atrophie blanche), and venous ulceration
The CEAP classification (Clinical, aEtiological, Anatomical, Pathophysiological) grades severity, with clinical classes C0 to C6, C6 being an active venous ulcer
Venous ulcers characteristically occur in the gaiter area around the medial malleolus, are shallow with irregular margins, and are often preceded by lipodermatosclerosis
Venous duplex ultrasound is the key investigation, mapping reflux and obstruction to guide treatment
Compression therapy is the cornerstone of management once significant arterial disease is excluded by the ankle-brachial pressure index; it promotes ulcer healing and prevents recurrence
Correcting superficial reflux by endovenous ablation (thermal or non-thermal) or surgery improves symptoms and ulcer healing in suitable patients
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic venous insufficiency stems from persistent ambulatory venous hypertension in the lower limb. Valvular incompetence in the superficial, deep, or perforating veins allows reflux, while venous outflow obstruction (for example after deep vein thrombosis) and calf-muscle pump failure also contribute. The elevated venous pressure is transmitted to the microcirculation, causing capillary leakage, fibrin deposition, leucocyte activation, and chronic inflammation. This produces oedema, characteristic skin changes such as haemosiderin staining and lipodermatosclerosis, and ultimately tissue breakdown and venous ulceration, typically in the gaiter region.
additionalDifferentials: Peripheral arterial disease or arterial ulcer
additionalInvestigations: Venous duplex ultrasound to map reflux and obstruction
Ankle-brachial pressure index to exclude significant arterial disease before compression
Photoplethysmography or venous filling assessment where indicated
Cross-sectional venography (CT or MR) for suspected proximal or iliac obstruction
Ulcer swab and, if atypical or non-healing, biopsy to exclude malignancy
Assessment for coexisting cardiac, renal, or hepatic causes of oedema
redFlags: A non-healing or atypical ulcer requiring biopsy to exclude malignancy (Marjolin's ulcer)
Coexisting significant arterial disease making compression hazardous
Signs of deep vein thrombosis or spreading cellulitis
A rapidly deteriorating limb or systemic sepsis
reference.prognosis: A chronic, relapsing condition; compression and correction of reflux heal most venous ulcers, but recurrence is common without ongoing compression and risk-factor control, and advanced skin changes are only partly reversible.
pitfalls: Applying compression without checking the ankle-brachial pressure index for arterial disease
Attributing all leg ulcers to venous disease and missing arterial, malignant, or vasculitic causes
Under-treating with inadequate compression, leading to non-healing
Neglecting to treat correctable superficial reflux
references: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
ESVS Clinical Practice Guidelines on Chronic Venous Disease
management: Graduated compression therapy as the mainstay, applied once significant arterial disease is excluded by the ankle-brachial pressure index, to heal ulcers and prevent recurrence
Ablation of superficial reflux by endovenous thermal ablation, foam sclerotherapy or surgical stripping, guided by duplex mapping
Venous stenting for deep or iliac outflow obstruction where appropriate

Adjunctive limb elevation, calf-muscle exercise, weight reduction and emollient skin care, with a topical corticosteroid for venous eczema and a venoactive agent such as micronised purified flavonoid fraction or pentoxifylline to aid ulcer healing
Venous ulcer wound management under compression, with biopsy of non-healing or atypical ulcers to exclude malignancy
Surveillance for ulcer recurrence and progression of skin changes, with ongoing maintenance compression
Referral to vascular services and exclusion of coexisting cardiac, renal or hepatic causes of oedema
